description: We’re a team of three Computer Engineering students and one AI enthusiast passionate about space exploration, artificial intelligence, and innovative technology. For NASA Space Apps, we're developing an intelligent lunar landing site selection system using NASA data, AI, and interactive visualizations. Our goal is to combine engineering, creativity, and science to solve real challenges in space exploration and push the boundaries of what's possible.
summary:
Plan Banana helps a lunar mission decide where and when to land, and what to do if the chosen spot turns out to be unsafe during descent. More than half of all lunar landing attempts have failed, and many recent failures were navigation problems.

We trained our own neural network on NASA LOLA terrain and 4 million simulated touchdowns near the lunar south pole. It predicts how likely a safe touchdown is for any spot. We combine that with physics checks for sunlight, battery power and Earth visibility, computed from JPL ephemerides. The web planner ranks landing regions and time windows, and marks a primary landing zone (Z1) and a backup (Z2), with a deadline for when the switch must be decided.

To show the second half of the idea, we built a 3D-printed lander prototype on an Arduino UNO Q. Its downward camera matches what it sees against a saved map of our foam Moon terrain, an IMU tracks its rotation, and when a hazard appears on Z1 it marks the zone not landable and redirects to Z2.

The planner will be open source for European researchers and small lunar teams.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Plan Banana answers the challenge question "where and when should we land?" for the lunar south pole, and adds a second one: "where do we go if that spot becomes unsafe on the way down?"

1. Mission planner (web dashboard). Pick a candidate region (for example Mons Mouton Plateau) and a date range. For every 250 m cell of a 15 x 15 km region the planner computes the safe-touchdown probability (our trained AI model) plus sunlight at touchdown, battery survival through a 6.5-day stay and Earth visibility for communication (deterministic physics from JPL DE421 and LOLA horizons). A cell is landable only if all four pass. Connected landable cells big enough for the landing uncertainty (180 m radius) become landing zones. The planner shows the best time window, a primary zone Z1, backup zones such as Z2, and how long before touchdown the switch must be decided.

2. Touchdown model. A Monte Carlo simulator runs 256 touchdowns per site on 20 m LOLA terrain (navigation error, hazard avoidance, sideways velocity, tip-over and slope limits). We simulated 16,000 south-polar sites, about 4 million touchdowns. An ensemble of five residual CNNs (342k parameters each) learns to correct a coarse 80 m physics estimate from a 32x32 terrain patch plus 13 terrain features. On a held-out longitude sector its mean error is 1.9 percentage points, versus 3.0 for the physics baseline.

3. Tabletop lander prototype. A 3D-printed rover with a clip-on sky-crane descent stage runs on an Arduino UNO Q with an IMX219 downward camera, a Modulino IMU and an OLED. The camera localizes against a saved map of our foam lunar terrain (SIFT matching, homography, optical flow) and the IMU tracks heading between camera fixes. Z1 and Z2 from the planner are loaded onto the board; a red marker on Z1 stands for a hazard seen during descent, and the system marks Z1 NOT LANDABLE and diverts to Z2.

4. Backup positioning (PNT). We tested Bluetooth beacons but got about 2 m error, too coarse for a tabletop. For real missions we point to NASA/ASI's LuGRE GNSS fix on the Moon and ESA's Moonlight programme.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
A failed lunar landing costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, and most recent failures were navigation problems. Plan Banana makes the landing plan adaptive: there is always a checked backup zone and a decision deadline. The planner will be open source for European university labs and small lunar teams, starting with the Turin space ecosystem.

TOOLS
Python, PyTorch, NumPy, Skyfield, FastAPI; Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js; OpenCV and Arduino App Lab on an Arduino UNO Q; Python CAD (trimesh, manifold3d), Bambu Studio and Blender.

LIMITATIONS
The model matches our simulator, not real flight outcomes. The tabletop hazard is a coloured marker, not lidar. The prototype hardware is not space-qualified. Next step: validate against real landing sites (Chang'e 3-6, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1).

Code: github.com/AlpMeteSenel/the-moonions (dashboard), the-moonions-backend (AI model), the-moonions-firmware (lander and hardware).

AI DISCLOSURE (SI)
Demo video: 3D animation and edit scripted with AI assistance (visible watermark); voice-over generated with ElevenLabs (AI voice). Code and slides were partly written with AI coding assistants and reviewed and tested by the team.
